newsitem.title: USA: A few hits helping record industry turn corner.
newsitem.headline: A few hits helping record industry turn corner.

text.p: A few hit acts helped record labels regain their balance in the latest quarter following a dizzying period of consolidation and downsizing throughout the $40 billion global music industry, analysts said Wednesday.

"Retail chains continue to demonstrate problems and disappointment, but we're beginning to see inroads by new artists and acts at the labels, which are beginning to get great play," said Chris Dixon, analyst with PaineWebber Inc.

For instance, results released by entertainment giant PolyGram NV Tuesday showed sales of veteran Irish rocker band U2's long-awaited album "Pop" and teen trio newcomers Hanson's hit album "Middle of Nowhere" helped offset PolyGram's growing film losses.

"Despite challenging conditions in some of our markets, PolyGram's expertise in breaking new acts and promotion of established artists is reflected in the first half results," said Chief Executive Alain Levy in a statement.
Music accounted for 87 percent of Polygram's revenues in the half year, with film contributing 13 percent.
PolyGram's first-half group sales rose 5 percent to $2.23 billion, including $1.94 billion in music sales. Operating profits from music rose to $257 million from $225 million.

According to Soundscan, a Hartsdale, N.Y.-based company that monitors retail music sales, overall U.S. album sales rose 5.4 percent in the first half of 1997, marking a turnaround for the $12 billion domestic music industry, which has seen flat sales for the past two years.
Soundscan said sales were led by the Spice Girls' debut album, "Spice," on EMI Group Plc's Virgin label and No Doubt's "Tragic Kingdom" on Trauma/Interscope.
Interscope is half-owned by Seagram Co. Ltd's Universal music group, which has jumped in market share this year with a roster of hot artists.
Universal and EMI have not yet reported results.

EMI, whose roster of artists ranges from The Beatles to the popular Spice Girls, had forecast only modest progress this year and has recently slashed jobs and shuttered some labels in a massive restructuring to boost its market share.
"Music labels are reporting a little better-than-expected results, indicating that demand for music as an entertainment medium remains intact," Dixon said.
John Penney, analyst with Sanford Bernstein, said he was cautiously optimistic for the world's music labels.

"As a group, the quarter has been mixed. Territories in Europe are still weak and we still have a way to go in the U.S. before the music patient is fully cured," said Penney, noting the 5.4 percent growth is concentrated on a few big acts and is a far cry from 11.2 percent growth in 1992.
In the past two years, hundreds of music retail stores have closed and many chains have declared bankruptcy after overexpansion, lack of runaway hits and brutal pricing wars.

The latest blow to the industry came last week when Alliance Entertainment, a distributor for hundreds of independent labels, filed for bankruptcy due to a growing debt load, coupled with a sluggish domestic sales market.

"The U.S. is showing unit growth, but that does not always translate into profitability. If promotional costs are not controlled, the industry risks seeing all unit gains vanish at the bottom line," Penney said.
Industry experts said a major restructuring paid off for Bertelsmann Music Group, which reported record revenue of $4.4 billion for the 1996-97 fiscal year after two years of restructuring.
Bertelsmann Music, home to the Arista and RCA labels, does not break out profits. But industry sources said they believed the label had record profits internationally and domestically.

Arista said it closed the year ended June 30, 1997 with sales exceeding $400 million and started the 1997 calendar year with record sales and profits. Among Arista's best sellers in the past year have been Toni Braxton's "Secrets" and Notorious B.I.G.'s posthumous "Life After Death."
Some analysts remain upbeat despite U.S. market leader Time Warner Inc. Warner Music's 24 percent drop in second-quarter earnings to $125 million from $165 million.
"They were down, but it was in line with expectations," said Dixon, noting the label, along with many others, has had problems at the distribution level.
"Not only do we have a combination of overabundance of retailers, we have some horrendous pricing policies that were put in place," said Dixon.

"Warner is considering alternative promotion schemes to try to build strength for its product," he said. Analysts also note that Warner is on the rebound with hit albums like Prodigy's "The Fat of the Land," on the Warner/Maverick label.

Sony Music, whose "Men in Black" soundtrack ranked No. 1 this week and last week, reports earnings July 31. Sony is expected to report flat to modest growth in the first quarter ended June 30 due to lack of major releases, although "Men in Black" and other new releases are expected to carry them into the next quarter.
